introduction-the-multi-account-reality.core: AWS accounts are the strongest isolation boundary for security, billing, quotas and blast radius. Mature organisations run dozens to thousands of accounts (per team, environment and workload). A landing zone is the well-architected multi-account foundation that makes this manageable, and Control Tower automates building and governing it.

first_principles.problem: Everything runs in one account, so a developer's mistake can delete production and costs can't be attributed.
truths: Accounts isolate permissions, quotas and billing.

analogy.title: Apartments in a managed building versus one shared house
analogy.story: Each tenant has their own locked flat; the building handles security, utilities and rules.
analogy.breaks: Flats are built once; accounts can be created in minutes.

example.title: Account strategy
flow: Workloads OU: prod and non-prod accounts per team

check.q: Why use many AWS accounts instead of one?
check.a: Accounts provide strong isolation of permissions, quotas, billing and blast radius.

the-landing-zone-what-gets-built.core: Control Tower's landing zone creates an AWS Organization with a Security OU containing a Log Archive account (centralised CloudTrail and Config logs) and an Audit account (security tooling, cross-account read access), sets up IAM Identity Center, an org-wide CloudTrail, Config aggregation and baseline guardrails, all in governed regions.

first_principles.problem: Building a secure multi-account baseline by hand takes months and drifts.
truths: Logs must be centralised and protected.
Baselines must apply to every account.

analogy.title: A new office park with security HQ and records room built first
analogy.story: Before tenants move in, the guardhouse and archive are ready.
analogy.breaks: Office parks don't update themselves; landing zones need version upgrades.

check.q: What are the two core accounts Control Tower creates in the Security OU?

the-account-vending-machine-account-fact.core: Account Factory provisions new accounts through Service Catalog or APIs, placing them into the right OU with baseline guardrails, networking and access already applied. Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) and Customizations for Control Tower (CfCT) add GitOps workflows and custom baselines (VPCs, roles, budgets) per account.

first_principles.problem: Requesting a new account takes weeks of tickets and manual setup, so teams share accounts instead.

analogy.title: A vending machine for fully furnished flats
analogy.story: Choose the size and floor; it comes with utilities, locks and rules already set.
analogy.breaks: Vending machines dispense instantly; account creation takes minutes plus baseline runs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: PR merged → governed account in under an hour.

check.a: Account Factory for Terraform: a GitOps pipeline for requesting and customising Control Tower accounts.

aws-organizations-ous-the-hierarchy.core: AWS Organizations arranges accounts in a tree of OUs under the root. Policies (SCPs, RCPs, tag policies, backup policies) attach to OUs and inherit downward. Design OUs by governance need (Security, Infrastructure, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/NonProd, Sandbox, Suspended), not by org chart, which changes often.

first_principles.problem: OUs mirror the company's departments, and every reorg requires reshuffling accounts and policies.
truths: Governance needs are more stable than org charts.

analogy.title: Building zones by safety rules, not by tenant company
analogy.story: Labs, offices and storage have different rules regardless of who rents them.
analogy.breaks: Building zones are physical; moving an account between OUs is a quick API call.

check.q: Why not mirror the org chart in OUs?
check.a: Org charts change often, while governance requirements (prod vs sandbox) are more stable.

service-control-policies-scps-the-guardr.core: SCPs attached to OUs cap what any principal in member accounts can do: deny disabling CloudTrail/Config/GuardDuty, deny leaving the organisation, restrict regions, deny root-user actions, require encryption or tags. They never grant permissions, and exceptions use conditions on trusted roles.

first_principles.problem: An account admin disables GuardDuty and CloudTrail to hide activity.
truths: Deny lists are easier to maintain than allow lists.

analogy.title: Building regulations that override tenants
analogy.story: Even the owner of a flat can't remove the fire alarms.
analogy.breaks: Regulations are enforced by inspection; SCPs are enforced on every API call.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No one can blind the security team.

check.a: No; they only set the maximum allowed permissions.

control-tower-guardrails-vs-scps-underst.core: Control Tower controls (guardrails) come in three types: preventive (implemented as SCPs or RCPs that block actions), detective (AWS Config rules that flag non-compliance) and proactive (CloudFormation hooks that block non-compliant resources before creation). They're managed, pre-built and reported in a dashboard, while raw SCPs are just one mechanism.

first_principles.problem: Teams think Control Tower guardrails and SCPs are the same and miss detective and proactive coverage.
truths: Some things should be blocked, others detected.
Managed controls reduce custom policy work.
derivation: Enable **mandatory, strongly recommended, elective** controls per OU.

analogy.title: Locks, cameras and building-plan reviews
analogy.story: Locks stop entry, cameras record problems and plan reviews reject unsafe designs before construction.
analogy.breaks: Plan reviews are manual; proactive controls run automatically on every deploy.

example.title: Layered controls for S3
flow: Preventive: deny disabling Block Public Access
Proactive: CFN hook rejects unencrypted buckets
Detective: Config flags public buckets created outside CFN
